Threat.value: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

vignette: Amira had always taken pride in her work as a housekeeper, moving quietly and efficiently through the grand homes she cleaned. But it was on one such job, three years ago, that everything changed. She remembered walking into the kitchen to start her routine when suddenly she was grabbed from behind and dragged to the floor. The sound of shouting still echoed in her mind - the man's angry voice, the thud of his fist against her head. What frightened her most was the feeling of being completely at his mercy, unable to move or escape. In the months that followed, Amira began to notice changes in herself. She had trouble concentrating on even the simplest tasks, and would often find herself zoning out mid-sentence. Her husband, Ali, would try to talk to her about their day, but she couldn't focus long enough to respond. At work, she'd catch herself scanning the rooms for signs of danger - checking the locks, peering into closets, listening for any unusual sounds. She knew it was irrational, but the memory of being trapped and helpless had left her with a constant sense of unease. As she went about her daily routine, Amira found herself avoiding situations where she might feel forced or restricted in some way. She would skip certain houses if they felt too isolated or had rooms that seemed too difficult to escape from. Her clients began to notice the change and started complaining about the quality of her work. Ali tried to reassure her that everything was okay, but Amira couldn't shake off the feeling of being on edge all the time. Reminders of victims would send her spiraling back into the memories of that day - a news report about an assault, a conversation with someone who had gone through something similar, even just seeing a person who resembled her attacker. These triggers left her reeling, and she'd often find herself curled up on the couch, unable to move or function. When the memories did come flooding back, Amira would relive the physical pain of that day - the ache in her head, the bruising on her skin. Some moments were crystal clear: the feeling of his hands around her throat, the sound of his voice in her ear. But others were hazy and unclear - she remembered being dragged across the floor, but not how she managed to get free. Lately, Amira had been noticing that her avoidance behaviors were taking a toll on her relationships and daily life. Ali was getting frustrated with her inability to focus or follow through on plans. Her clients were canceling appointments due to her inconsistent work quality. And yet, the thought of confronting these issues head-on filled her with dread. What finally brought Amira to seek help was the realization that she couldn't keep living like this - constantly scanning for danger, avoiding anything that might trigger a memory. She knew it wasn't rational, but she was certain that if she didn't find a way to manage these symptoms, they would consume her completely. As she sat in the therapist's office, fidgeting with her hands and trying to put into words what had been happening, Amira felt a glimmer of hope - maybe, just maybe, there was a way out of this never-ending cycle of fear and avoidance.
